ops.rationale: Splits the two ideas of the first sentence, says what the 30-day blanking window does where it first appears, and defines the ECG term at its first use; every number and claim kept.
Uses incident AF and AUROC as the one term for each concept and splits the paragraph at its second idea, the outcome definition; numbers and citations unchanged.
ops.new_text:
Deep networks trained on sinus-rhythm ECGs predict incident AF. A network trained on 1.6 million ECGs reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.85 for incident AF within one year \cite{Raghunath_2021}. When an ECG network and CHARGE-AF were combined, discrimination was highest for the combination in an internal and two external test sets \cite{Khurshid_2022}. The ECG and the clinical risk factors therefore carry partly different information.

Reported performance also depends on how the outcome is defined. A systematic review of 14 studies found a median AUROC of 0.740, with higher values for 31-day confirmation windows than for 1-year windows (0.851 against 0.630) \cite{Tsiartas_2025}. Eleven of these studies cited possible misclassification of negative cases. A model of incident AF therefore has to be judged with its outcome window and its label source stated.

ops.rationale: Adds the sentence that connects the guideline statement to the paragraph's claim, through the interpretability barrier the cited review already names.
ops.new_text: The networks behind these results are black boxes, and their explanations are computed after training. A commentary on predicting incident AF in sinus rhythm is subtitled ``more than just trusting the `black box'\,'' \cite{Kashou_2021}, and a narrative review names interpretability as a barrier to clinical use \cite{Saiz_Vivo_2025}. The 2024 guideline of the European Society of Cardiology addresses the neighbouring task of automated AF diagnosis. It states that the clinical performance and broad applicability of such algorithms are not yet known \cite{Van_Gelder_2024}. The guideline thus leaves open whether such algorithms perform in clinical use, and the narrative review counts their limited interpretability among the barriers to that use. The explanations themselves are uncertain. Twelve attribution methods applied to ECG classifiers agreed poorly and were only moderately consistent across training runs for most methods \cite{Arends_2026}. For some of these methods, randomising the weights of the network did not remove the attribution pattern entirely. An explanation of this kind may describe the attribution method as much as the model. Rudin argued that a model for high-stakes decisions should be interpretable by design, instead of a black box explained afterwards \cite{Rudin_2019}. For incident AF, such a model would have to keep the discrimination of a deep network while exposing what it reads from the ECG.

ops.rationale: Defines mode, low-rank factor and Grad-CAM at their first appearance; the Grad-CAM clause stays here and its repeat in Related work is reworded in OP016.
ops.new_text: Block-term tensor models offer one route to such a model. A block-term decomposition splits a multiway signal into blocks with low-rank factors per mode \cite{De_Lathauwer_2008}. A mode is one axis of the multiway array, such as frequency, time or lead, and a low-rank factor is a matrix with few columns, so that the block describes its mode by a few components. In neural networks, block-term structure has compressed weight matrices, and those networks are explained with Grad-CAM maps instead of through their factors \cite{arxiv_2010_04963}. Grad-CAM weights the feature maps of a convolutional layer by the gradient of the output and so marks the input regions that most raise the output. In supervised regression of brain signals, block-term tensor regression, designed for interpretability, predicted finger movements \cite{Faes_2024}. That regression is linear and has no survival objective, which incident prediction with censored follow-up needs. To our knowledge, no published model places readable block-term frequency and lead factors on the predictive path of a survival network for incident AF. Such a model would also need a way to add clinical risk factors, which complement the ECG \cite{Khurshid_2022}. The clinical factors should not enter the factors that are meant to be read, or the reading would mix the two sources.

ops.rationale: Names the comparator the clinical model, as elsewhere, and states the authors' decision on ECG-read labels with we.
ops.new_text: This study addresses two questions. The first is whether a block-term tensor network predicts incident AF from one sinus-rhythm 12-lead ECG more accurately than a clinical model and a convolutional neural network (CNN). In this network, the ECG evidence passes through readable frequency and lead factors. Age, sex and ECG intervals enter through a separate linear term. The second question is where in the cardiac cycle the ECG evidence of the network lies. We answer both questions in MIMIC-IV-ECG, with incident AF defined from hospital diagnoses coded in the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). We did not use labels read from the ECG as outcomes, since a third of a sample of 700 AF-labelled ECGs of this database did not show AF on expert review (Section~\ref{sec:cohort}) \cite{Valasakis_2026}. All methods share one cohort, one set of folds and one set of risk factors. Differences between them are therefore differences of model.

ops.rationale: Says what the blanking window does in the cohort contribution and splits the 39-word item into its two independent contributions.
ops.new_text:
The contributions of the study are these:
\begin{itemize}
\item BTTN, a survival network whose ECG evidence passes through per-block frequency and lead factors, with a separate linear clinical term that does not pass through those factors.
\item An incident-AF cohort in MIMIC-IV-ECG defined from ICD-coded hospital diagnoses, reported with its exclusion counts. The cohort excludes as prevalent or concurrent the patients with an AF diagnosis, or an ECG read as AF, before the end of a 30-day blanking window after the index ECG.
\item A comparison of one-year discrimination against a clinical model, a CNN and linear block-term tensor regression (BTTR) under one protocol.
\item The discrimination of BTTN at four horizons, read from the same cross-validated risks without refitting for each horizon.
\item The calibration, risk stratification and operating points of BTTN with the clinical term.
\item A beat-aligned, energy-normalised occlusion profile of the ECG term of BTTN.
\end{itemize}

ops.rationale: Writes AUC as AUROC, the term defined in the Introduction.
ops.new_text: Two tasks are reported under the heading of AF prediction from the sinus-rhythm ECG, and they differ in what counts as a case. In identification, a case is a patient who already has AF or shows it soon after the ECG. A CNN developed on 649,931 sinus-rhythm ECGs of 180,922 Mayo Clinic patients, 454,789 of them in its training set, identified patients with AF with an AUROC of 0.87, counting AF before the tested ECG as positive \cite{Attia_2019}. A network for AF within 31 days of a sinus-rhythm ECG reached AUROCs of 0.86 on held-out Veterans Affairs ECGs and 0.93 at a non-VA site \cite{Yuan_2023}. In incident prediction, a case is a patient whose first AF follows the ECG after a stated interval. The two tasks give different numbers. In a systematic review, models with 31-day confirmation windows had higher median AUROCs than models with 1-year windows \cite{Tsiartas_2025}, and a narrative review found AI more accurate at shorter event horizons \cite{Saiz_Vivo_2025}. The present study addresses incident prediction only.

ops.rationale: Breaks the six repeated 'model reached value' sentences into varied shapes and uses incident AF, AUROC and C-index as the one term for each concept; every value and citation kept.
ops.new_text: Studies of dated incident AF report lower values. Raghunath et al.\ reported an AUROC of 0.85 for incident AF within one year on ECGs from 430,000 patients \cite{Raghunath_2021}. For a model from a Montreal cardiac centre, the AUROC was 0.78 at five years and 0.77 on external validation in MIMIC-IV \cite{Jabbour_2024}. Its abstract does not state the label source used in MIMIC-IV. On the hospital from which MIMIC-IV comes, the C-index was 0.750 for a CNN trained with a discrete-time survival loss \cite{Sau_2026} and 0.754 for a model of ECG images \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. In Brazilian telehealth data, the data family of an earlier 12-lead diagnostic network \cite{Ribeiro_2020}, a residual CNN with survival analysis had an AUROC of 0.845 \cite{Habineza_2023}. With a mean follow-up of 80 days, a gradient-boosting survival model of 417 engineered ECG features gave a C-index of 0.781 \cite{Riek_2026}. These designs differ in horizon, population and label source, so their values do not rank the models.

ops.rationale: Rewrites the closing gap sentence out of the repeated 'To our knowledge, no...' template, keeping its hedge and its claim.
ops.new_text: The explanations in these studies are computed after training. Saliency mapping gave the P-wave the greatest influence in one ECG network \cite{Khurshid_2022}. Saliency of the image model focused on P-wave morphology and the PR interval \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. The feature-based model named lower P-wave amplitude among its predictors \cite{Riek_2026}. These reports agree on the atrial part of the beat. We found no test, in these reports, of whether the explanation reflects what the model uses to predict.

ops.rationale: Writes the concordance measure as C-index, the one term used for it.
ops.new_text: Clinical risk models set the comparator that an ECG model has to match. The Framingham score predicted 10-year AF from age, sex, a heart murmur, heart failure, systolic blood pressure, hypertension treatment, body mass index and the PR interval, with a C-index of 0.78 \cite{Schnabel_2009}. CHARGE-AF reached 0.765 at derivation and 0.664 and 0.705 in two validation cohorts \cite{Alonso_2013}. Adding ECG variables did not improve its discrimination. ECG intervals measured in sinus rhythm are nevertheless AF predictors in their own right. In Framingham, each 20 ms increment of the PR interval carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.12 for AF \cite{Cheng_2009}. Across Framingham and ARIC, a P-wave duration above 120 ms was associated with AF (hazard ratio 1.55), but P-wave indices added little discrimination beyond traditional risk factors \cite{Magnani_2015}. These results motivate the ECG intervals in the clinical term of this study. They also set a modest expectation for what interval measurements alone add.

ops.rationale: Writes C statistics as C-indices, the one term used for the concordance measure.
ops.new_text: Studies that combined an ECG network with clinical factors found the two complementary in most cohorts. AUROC was comparable for CHARGE-AF and an ECG network in three test sets and highest for their combination, at 0.838, 0.777 and 0.746 \cite{Khurshid_2022}. In an older community cohort, an AI-ECG and CHARGE-AF had equal C-indices of 0.69, predicted AF independently, and reached 0.72 together \cite{Christopoulos_2020}. A single-lead ECG model with age and sex had an AUROC of 0.695 against 0.679 for CHARGE-AF in trial data \cite{Khurshid_2025}. A random forest that combined demographic, clinical, engineered and deep ECG features reached 0.909, against 0.839 for the best single modality \cite{Biton_2021}.

ops.rationale: Writes AUC as AUROC.
ops.new_text: Other studies found the ECG model ahead of the clinical score. In 2,301 patients of a Montreal cohort, an ECG model exceeded CHARGE-AF, which reached an AUROC of 0.62, and an AF polygenic score, which reached 0.59 \cite{Jabbour_2024}. An image-based ECG model reached 0.696 against 0.667 for CHARGE-AF, and 0.711 when the two were combined \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. The ranking of ECG and clinical models also depends on the cohort. An ECG model led in hospital patients, while CHARGE-AF was the best single predictor in UK Biobank \cite{Sau_2026}. Fusing the two sources is therefore supported, but the way the fusion is built decides whether the ECG part can still be read.

ops.rationale: Defines remove-and-retrain evaluation at its first use from the cited benchmark, whose read passage says ROAR replaces the inputs estimated most important with a fixed uninformative value.
ops.new_text: Post-hoc explanations have been put to tests, and several methods fail them. Tests that randomise the model parameters and the training labels showed some saliency methods to be independent of both the model and the data-generating process \cite{arxiv_1810_03292}. Remove-and-retrain evaluation replaces the inputs that an attribution method ranks most important with an uninformative value, retrains the model and measures how far its accuracy falls \cite{arxiv_1806_10758}. Under this evaluation, only VarGrad and SmoothGrad-Squared, of the methods tested, did better than a random assignment of importance \cite{arxiv_1806_10758}. On the ECG, twelve attribution methods agreed poorly with one another \cite{Arends_2026}. Their self-consistency across initialisations was moderate for most methods, with mean correlations of 0.41 to 0.65. Dataset-level auditing with sanity checks gives a more favourable reading, in which aggregated saliency aligned with the decision rules of cardiologists \cite{Wagner_2024}. In that work the same methods also supported knowledge discovery, such as subtypes of myocardial infarction. The balance of this evidence leaves any explanation computed after training open to doubt about what it shows. It motivates models whose readable parts lie on the path of the prediction itself.

ops.rationale: Defines leakage as the encoding of information beyond the named concepts that the paragraph reports, before the term is used.
ops.new_text: Such models route the prediction through parts that can be read. Concept bottleneck models first predict named concepts and then the label, at accuracy competitive with end-to-end models \cite{arxiv_2007_04612}. Correcting the predicted concepts at test time raised their accuracy, which shows one use of a readable intermediate layer. Their concept representations can, however, encode information beyond the named concepts, which makes the reading of the downstream prediction misleading \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. B-cos networks summarise the full computation as one linear transform at similar ImageNet accuracy \cite{arxiv_2205_10268}. An anti-aliased variant gave explanations without artifacts on chest x-rays while keeping its predictive performance \cite{arxiv_2507_16761}. The multilinear structure of tensor networks has also been combined with deep networks, in preliminary results, to give weight-based interpretability at accuracy equal to baselines \cite{arxiv_2504_02667}. We call the encoding of information beyond the named concepts leakage. Leakage bears on any nonlinear head placed on readable factors, including the head of the model in this study.

ops.rationale: Rewrites the gap sentence out of the repeated 'To our knowledge, no...' template, scoped to the studies reviewed, with the same claim.
ops.new_text: Whether intrinsic interpretability costs accuracy on the ECG is contested. A study of variational-autoencoder representations of interpretable ECG features reported a cost of intrinsic explainability \cite{Patlatzoglou_2025}. A supervised block-term discriminant method reported none on EEG decoding, with a mean accuracy of 64.52\% against 61.00\% for its predecessor, higher-order discriminant analysis, on motor imagery \cite{arxiv_2511_04292}. Image networks that are interpretable by design also kept their accuracy \cite{arxiv_2205_10268,arxiv_2507_16761}. The answer may depend on the model family and on the task. None of the studies reviewed here compares an intrinsically interpretable model with a CNN on incident AF under one protocol. That comparison is one aim of the present work.

ops.rationale: Opens on the paragraph's point, defines multilinear rank and the CP and Tucker decompositions (CP and Tucker in the words of the Kolda abstract read in the run), rewords the repeated Grad-CAM clause and drops the 'is a different model' and 'instead of' contrasts.
ops.new_text: The uses of block-term structure differ in where the factors sit: in the weights of a network, within a recording, or on the input of a predictive model. Each use rests on the block-term decomposition, which writes a tensor as a sum of blocks of low multilinear rank, that is, blocks that each need only a few components along each mode \cite{De_Lathauwer_2008}. It contains the CP and Tucker decompositions as special cases \cite{De_Lathauwer_2008}. The CP decomposition writes a tensor as a sum of rank-one tensors, and the Tucker decomposition is a higher-order form of principal component analysis, as a survey of both describes \cite{Kolda_2009}. Block-term tensor neural networks approximate the weight matrices of CNNs and recurrent networks by block-term tensors to compress them, and their authors explain the compressed networks with Grad-CAM \cite{arxiv_2010_04963}. The model of this paper shares part of that name. Its factors act on the input and can be read. On AF ECGs, a regularised block-term decomposition extracted several signals interpretable as AF patterns \cite{Goulart_2020}. That work separates sources within a recording and does not predict risk.

ops.rationale: Defines deflation, writes ROC-AUC as AUROC, and replaces the second statement of the gap (kept in the Introduction) with the link to the Method that names the block-term layer.
ops.new_text: Supervised block-term models extract factors that both predict and can be read. Block-term tensor regression (BTTR) predicted finger trajectories from intracranial recordings, with automatic extraction of its components \cite{Faes_2024}. A block-term discriminant analysis gave interpretable and efficient dimensionality reduction for brain-computer interfaces, with an AUROC of 91.25\% on event-related potentials \cite{arxiv_2511_04292}. Linear BTTR has also been applied to the identification of AF in sinus rhythm on the median beat \cite{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22227432}, which is a different task from dated incidence. These models fit their blocks by deflation, which fits one block, subtracts its fit from the data and fits the next block to the remainder. They score linearly and have no time-to-event objective. BTTN, described next, trains readable block-term frequency and lead factors end to end with a survival objective and keeps the clinical factors outside the block-term layer.

ops.rationale: Supports the claim that the magnitude spectrogram needs no beat alignment with the standard shift property of the Fourier transform; the claim itself unchanged.
ops.new_text: Each index ECG is a 10-second, 12-lead recording sampled at 500 Hz \cite{https://doi.org/10.13026/4nqg-sb35}. Each lead was high-pass filtered at 0.5 Hz with a second-order filter and notch filtered at 50 Hz. It was then denoised by soft thresholding of a three-level sym4 wavelet decomposition, decimated to 250 Hz, centred, and scaled by its maximum absolute value. A magnitude spectrogram was computed per lead with a 128-sample window (512 ms) and a 32-sample hop (128 ms). Frequencies up to 40 Hz were kept, magnitudes were transformed by $\log(1+x)$, and the time axis was resampled to 40 frames. Mains interference at 60 Hz, the mains frequency of the source hospital, therefore lies outside the kept band. The result is a tensor $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times T \times L}$ with $F = 21$ frequency bins from 0 to 39 Hz, 1.95 Hz apart, $T = 40$ time frames and $L = 12$ leads, standardised per recording. Within each training fold, each lead was standardised again with the statistics of the training patients. A time shift of a signal changes the phase of its Fourier transform and leaves the magnitude unchanged. A magnitude spectrogram therefore changes little when the beat shifts within a window, so beats need no alignment across recordings.

ops.rationale: Defines a mode-n fibre where the mode-n product first uses it.
Defines the anchor age from the MIMIC-IV description already cited (the anchor_age passage and its shifted-year example read in the run).
Removes the second statement that the head's use of the factors is not measured; that limitation and its citation stand once, in the Limitations (OP040).
ops.new_text: This construction makes the factors readable by design and keeps the clinical term out of them. In this paper, readable names this property of the factors of a model that is interpretable by design. It is the sense in which the title calls BTTN interpretable. Every path from the ECG to the risk passes through the block projections of Equation~\eqref{eq:block}. The frequency and lead factors are therefore parameters on which the prediction depends, and they can be read directly. The clinical term reaches the log-risk without passing through the block-term layer. Adding it leaves the role of the factors unchanged, and the risk factors can be read as a linear term beside the ECG evidence. Readability is here a property of the architecture, and this study reports no reading of the learned frequency and lead factors.

ops.rationale: States the two outcome decisions of the authors with we.
ops.new_text: The cohort comes from MIMIC-IV-ECG, about 800,000 diagnostic ECGs from nearly 160,000 patients \cite{https://doi.org/10.13026/4nqg-sb35}. It is linked to the hospital module of MIMIC-IV, drawn from the electronic health record of the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center \cite{Johnson_2023}. Incident AF is the first hospital admission with a diagnosis of AF or flutter (ICD-10 I48, or ICD-9 427.31 or 427.32 for older admissions), dated by its admission time. We counted AF and flutter together, since a coded flutter diagnosis did not reliably separate flutter from AF in a registry validation \cite{Rix_2012}. We preferred hospital diagnoses to labels read from the ECG, since only 65.4\% of 700 AF-labelled ECGs in MIMIC-IV showed AF on expert review \cite{Valasakis_2026}.

ops.rationale: Reports the fitting of the CNN in the past tense, as the rest of the paragraph does.
ops.new_text: Three baselines shared the cohort, folds and inputs of BTTN. The clinical model is a class-balanced logistic regression on the nine factors of the clinical term, with median imputation and standardisation. Linear BTTR \cite{Faes_2024} was fitted on the same spectral tensor to the label coded as $-1$ and $+1$, with up to eight blocks. The CNN applies three one-dimensional convolutional layers of 32, 64 and 64 channels along time, with frequency and lead flattened into input channels. With batch normalisation, dropout and global average pooling, it was trained with weighted cross-entropy and early stopping as a three-member ensemble. In the survival design, the clinical baseline is a Cox model with a ridge penalty of 0.1 on the same factors.

ops.rationale: Splits the paragraph at its second idea, the calibration and clinical-use measures, and defines cross-fitting and net benefit (from the decision curve analysis already cited) where they first appear.
ops.new_text:
The one-year comparison used stratified five-fold cross-validation at the patient level, repeated over five seeds, with each patient's scores averaged over seeds. The survival model used one stratified five-fold split, with an event within one year as the label for early stopping. Each patient's risk in the survival design came from the fold in which that patient was held out. The clinical Cox model was fitted on the same training folds as the networks. AUROC intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples with percentile limits. At each horizon, cases had an event by the horizon and controls were AF-free beyond it, and patients censored earlier were excluded.

Calibration and clinical use were assessed at one year in the survival sample, after two-fold cross-fitted logistic recalibration. Cross-fitting splits the sample into two halves, fits the recalibration on one half, applies it to the other, and then swaps the halves. Calibration and clinical use were measured by Brier scores, decision curves \cite{Vickers_2006} and operating points at the top 5, 10, 20 and 30\% of risk. A decision curve plots net benefit against the threshold probability at which a patient would be treated. Net benefit is the proportion of true positives minus the proportion of false positives, weighted by the odds of the threshold probability \cite{Vickers_2006}. Positive predictive value (PPV) and the number needed to monitor, its inverse, were recomputed at the proportion of cases among the cases and AF-free controls of the one-year design, 1,855 in 43,625. We report the study with reference to the TRIPOD+AI statement \cite{Collins_2024}, without a table of participant characteristics and without counts of missing values per clinical factor.

ops.rationale: Removes the second idea, how the readout's choices shape the result, whose cited clauses stand once in the Limitations (OP040), and points to that place.
ops.new_text: The offsets from 225 ms before to 375 ms after the R peak were grouped into five windows, the P, PR, QRS, ST and T windows. Table~\ref{tab:occlusion} gives the offsets each window contains and the span of the beat that their occlusions cover. The offsets from 350 to 250 ms before the R peak and at 400 and 425 ms after it belong to no window. They are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:beat-saliency}, and their removed energy counts in the mean energy over all leads and offsets that the normalisation adds. They enter no window value. These windows are fixed offsets and are not delineated per beat. A negative mean drop at a lead and offset was set to zero before the window means were taken, for both the raw and the normalised value. The profile of a window is the mean over leads and over the offsets it contains. The zero replacement and the 24 ms window are choices of this readout, and the limitations discuss how such choices shape the profile. The readout describes the fitted model on its own training ECGs.

ops.rationale: States the authors' reporting decision with we.
ops.new_text: In the one-year design, the fused model had the highest AUROC of the methods compared, 0.7776 (95\% CI [0.7664, 0.7888]) (Table~\ref{tab:oneyear}). Its interval lay above the CNN's interval of [0.7226, 0.7469]. It also lay above the interval of ECG-only BTTN, 0.7397 [0.7275, 0.7517], so the fused model discriminated better than ECG-only BTTN. The fused model's interval overlapped the interval of the clinical model, 0.7597 [0.7488, 0.7713]. The study reports no paired interval for the difference between the fused and clinical models, so we report their estimates side by side. The CNN reached 0.7350, with an interval that overlapped that of ECG-only BTTN, so the two are comparable on this cohort. ECG-only BTTN exceeded linear BTTR, at 0.5967 [0.5824, 0.6115], with intervals that do not overlap.

ops.rationale: Opens on the paragraph's point, that the fused model stays above the clinical Cox model at each horizon; the procedure follows and every value is kept.
ops.new_text: In the survival design, the fused model had point estimates above those of the clinical Cox model at each horizon (Table~\ref{tab:horizons}). The same cross-validated risks were read at every horizon without refitting. The fused model had an AUROC of 0.723 [0.701, 0.745] at 120 days, for onset in the 90 days after the blanking window, 31 to 120 days after the index ECG. Its AUROC was 0.727 [0.711, 0.743] at one year, 0.740 [0.727, 0.753] at two years and 0.745 [0.735, 0.755] at five years. The clinical Cox model had point estimates of 0.710, 0.711, 0.727 and 0.731. ECG-only BTTN ranged from 0.658 to 0.676. The four horizons share the same risks and overlapping patients. They describe the behaviour of each model and are not independent replications. One reason for the lower one-year values of the survival design is its control group. At one year it includes patients who develop AF later, whereas the controls of the one-year design have no AF diagnosis.

ops.rationale: Replaces 'close in most deciles' with the largest gap the paragraph already reports, and follows the Brier scores with what they show; no number added.
ops.new_text: After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, the largest gap between the predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model lay in the sixth decile, among 19,986 patients with 838 cases (Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}). In that decile (bar 5 of Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}), 4.95\% was observed against a mean prediction of 3.56\%. The deciles are read in the survival sample, which holds a larger share of the events of the cohort than of its controls (4,000 of 8,775 against 16,000 of 41,770). Its proportions of AF are therefore higher than those of the cohort. Observed one-year AF rose from 0.55\% in the lowest decile to 11.4\% in the highest, with mean predicted risks of 0.61\% and 12.3\%. The sixth decile also had a higher observed proportion than the seventh (bar 6, 4.15\%). Brier scores, the mean squared difference between the predicted probability and the outcome, were 0.0390 for the fused model, 0.0396 for ECG-only BTTN and 0.0398 for the clinical model. The fused model thus had the lowest Brier score of the three, although the three scores differ only in the fourth decimal place.

ops.rationale: Joins the two short clinical-use paragraphs into one that opens on its point and drops the sentence describing the paragraph; every threshold and value kept.
ops.new_text: Sensitivity and PPV were higher for the fused model than for the clinical model at all four flagged fractions (Table~\ref{tab:operating}). At the top 10\% of risk, the fused model had a sensitivity of 0.272 against 0.240 for the clinical model, at specificities of 0.908 and 0.906. At the proportion of cases in the one-year design, its PPV was 0.1155 against 0.1019, a number needed to monitor of 8.7 against 9.8. In the decision curves of Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}, the curve of the fused model lay above the other two between threshold probabilities of about 0.03 and 0.12. All three models had a net benefit above both treating all and treating none at threshold probabilities from about 0.04 to about 0.1. Below about 0.04, their curves lay close to that of treating all, and all curves lay near zero above about 0.12.

ops.rationale: Its decision-curve content is joined into the paragraph of OP029.
Every claim of this paragraph stands in the Results and again in the Conclusion; deleting it ends the mirror of the Conclusion and the terms it cycled.
Gives the new first paragraph of the Discussion an antecedent for its values, and splits the 33-word foundation-model sentence; claims and citations kept.
ops.new_text: Published results give context for the discrimination of the fused model within one health system. On the hospital behind MIMIC-IV, a survival-loss CNN reached a C-index of 0.750 \cite{Sau_2026} and an image-based model 0.754 \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. A Montreal model reached an AUROC of 0.77 on external validation in MIMIC-IV, with a label source that its abstract does not state \cite{Jabbour_2024}. Elsewhere, an AUROC of 0.85 at one year \cite{Raghunath_2021} and a C-index of 0.781 over a short follow-up \cite{Riek_2026} were reported. These studies differ from the present one in horizon, outcome definition, sample and metric. A systematic review shows how far such choices move reported values \cite{Tsiartas_2025}. Identification studies \cite{Attia_2019,Yuan_2023} address another task. So does AF diagnosis from the ECG. A foundation model reported an AUROC of 0.996 for the AF label of multi-label ECG interpretation \cite{McKeen_2025}. Its authors also released an open benchmark on MIMIC-IV-ECG \cite{McKeen_2025}.

ops.rationale: Names the fused model in place of the ambiguous 'Its', splits the paragraph at its second idea (ECG-only BTTN against the CNN) and uses the term ECG-only BTTN.
ops.new_text:
The gain of the fused model over the clinical model agrees with reports that ECG and clinical information are complementary \cite{Khurshid_2022,Christopoulos_2020}. The operating point of the fused model at the top 10\% of risk is of the same order as that of one externally validated model. That model flagged 9.7\% of older patients with a sensitivity of 31\% and a specificity of 92\%, in a different population with chart-confirmed endpoints \cite{Pfeifer_2026}.

The comparability of ECG-only BTTN with the CNN bears on the reported accuracy cost of intrinsic interpretability on the ECG \cite{Patlatzoglou_2025}. In this design, ECG-only BTTN, built on readable factors, reached the discrimination of a compact CNN. The CNN has three convolutional layers, so the result says nothing about parity with the large networks of published work.

ops.rationale: Removes the repeat of 'this study reports no reading of the factors', which stands in the Method (OP021), and writes factor layer as block-term layer.
ops.new_text: Separating the clinical term from the block-term layer lets the fused model gain discrimination without passing the risk factors through its ECG factors. The ECG evidence still passes through frequency and lead factors, and each risk factor enters the linear term with one weight. The two sources therefore have separate parameters that can be inspected apart. The fused model is trained as one network, so its factors are fitted beside the clinical term and may differ from those of ECG-only BTTN. In a fused network whose clinical inputs enter the block-term layer, the factors could absorb risk-factor information, as concept representations absorb information beyond their concepts \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. The architecture of BTTN closes this route for the clinical term. It does not close it for information that the ECG itself carries, which the factors may encode in ways a reader does not expect.

ops.rationale: Replaces the template limits opener with the paragraph's point, keeps the two limits of the agreement in it, and moves the third idea, the hypothesis on the fused gain, to the next paragraph (OP036).
ops.new_text: The agreement with the cohort studies is partial in two respects. First, in a Swedish cohort of 70-year-olds, the PR interval measured in lead V1 was not related to incident AF, while a short P-wave duration was \cite{Ostrowska_2022}. Second, the cohort studies measure the PR interval from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex. The PR window of the readout instead groups the occlusions centred 125 to 75 ms before the R peak, a fixed span from 136 to 62 ms before it. On the mean beat of Figure~\ref{fig:beat-saliency}, this span holds the end of the P wave and the PR segment. The agreement claimed here therefore concerns the location within the cardiac cycle only.

ops.rationale: Joins the two atrial hypotheses into one paragraph that ends once, and states the authors' offering of them with we; both readings, their hedges and citations kept.
ops.new_text: Two readings of these results concern the atria, and we offer both as hypotheses. The clinical term holds P-wave duration but no PR interval. One reading of the gain of the fused model is that the ECG term carries information on atrial and atrioventricular conduction that the clinical term does not measure. The second reading rests on a clinical frame for an atrial focus. An expert consensus defines atrial cardiomyopathy as structural, architectural, contractile or electrophysiological changes of the atria that can produce clinically relevant manifestations, among them arrhythmia \cite{Goette_2016}. In a Japanese community cohort, prolonged P-wave duration was associated both with incident AF and with more left atrial fibrosis at autopsy \cite{Maezono_2025}. In this reading, the PR-window response reflects such atrial change. The present results test neither reading. Testing the second needs studies that pair the ECG with measurements of the atrium.

ops.rationale: Splits the single-database limit from the label limit, states the follow-up requirement as a selection limitation with the counts of the cohort table, and takes in the missing participant table moved from the calibration paragraph.
ops.new_text:
The study used one database from one health system and has no external validation in a cohort with dated outcomes. Its cohort is also selected by follow-up. Controls needed at least 365 days of follow-up, and 88,945 of the 151,941 eligible patients had no AF and follow-up under 365 days (Table~\ref{tab:cohort}). Patients with a year of follow-up in this health system may differ from those without, so this requirement may bias the estimates of discrimination and calibration. The study also reports no table of the characteristics of cases and controls and no count of missing values per clinical factor. The sample therefore cannot be compared with another population on these measures.

The labels of the study are ICD-coded hospital diagnoses, which are mostly correct but incomplete. A meta-analysis of 24 validation studies pooled a PPV of 88\% and a sensitivity of 80\% for administrative AF definitions \cite{Yao_2019}. In a population study, a hospital discharge diagnosis found 73.7\% of record-verified AF, with a PPV of 88.5\% \cite{Malmo_2016}. A registry found a PPV of 92.6\% for the combined AF or flutter diagnosis \cite{Rix_2012}. Some controls may therefore have AF diagnosed only outside hospital. Onset is dated by the admission and not by the first occurrence of AF. Follow-up to death counts patients without a hospital AF diagnosis as AF-free.

ops.rationale: Replaces the template limits opener with the paragraph's point and writes clinical comparator as clinical model; the restating close is folded into the opener.
ops.new_text: The clinical model is narrower and less exact than a full clinical score. Age is the anchor age of MIMIC-IV, which is not the age at the index ECG \cite{Johnson_2023}. The clinical factors omit variables of the Framingham score, among them systolic blood pressure, hypertension treatment, body mass index and heart failure \cite{Schnabel_2009}. They also omit the PR interval, a known AF predictor \cite{Cheng_2009,Magnani_2013}. The CNN baseline is compact, and a larger network might reach a different value.

ops.rationale: Replaces the template limits opener with the paragraph's point and moves its second idea, the missing participant table, to OP037.
ops.new_text: The calibration and the PPVs hold for the samples in which they were estimated. The probabilities were recalibrated in the evaluation sample with two-fold cross-fitting, so the calibration of the model in another population is not shown. The one-year design sampled four controls per case, and the survival design sampled cases and controls. PPV was therefore recomputed at the proportion of cases among the cases and AF-free controls of the one-year design, 1,855 in 43,625. This proportion exceeds the one-year rate of the survival cohort, 1,855 in 50,545, whose one-year negatives include the patients with onset after one year. The PPVs of Table~\ref{tab:operating} are therefore upper values for that population.

ops.rationale: Keeps the cited readout-choice clauses here as their one statement, adds the energy normalisation as an alternative explanation of the window order, stated as a limitation, and splits off the head's use of the factors as its own paragraph.
ops.new_text:
The occlusion readout is a perturbation explanation of the fitted model on 120 high-risk training ECGs. It is open to the critiques of post-hoc attribution \cite{arxiv_1810_03292,arxiv_1806_10758,Arends_2026}. Its zero replacement, its 24 ms window and its fixed windows relative to the R peak shape the profile, since the replacement value and the window size shape an occlusion map \cite{arxiv_1702_04595}. The perturbation method and the region size likewise shape the evaluation of attributions on time series \cite{_imi__2025}. Another replacement could change the order of the windows. The energy normalisation may also shape that order. Division by the removed energy favours windows of low energy, so the PR window may rank first in part because occluding it removes little energy.

Readable factors do not by themselves show that the nonlinear head routes its decision through them in the way their reading suggests \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. The readability of BTTN rests on its architecture, and this study reports no measurement of how far the factors carry the decision on ICD-coded labels.

ops.rationale: Sets the five extensions as a list introduced with a colon, defines transport where it is used, and names the hypothetical comparator a clinical model.
ops.new_text:
These studies would extend this work:
\begin{itemize}
\item A test of the block factors on ICD-coded labels would measure how far the factors carry the decision. It would use control probes and the removal of top-ranked against bottom-ranked factors, in the manner of remove-and-retrain evaluation \cite{arxiv_1806_10758}.
\item External validation in a cohort with dated outcomes, and temporal validation within MIMIC-IV, would test whether the model transports, that is, whether its discrimination and calibration hold in a population or period other than the one it was developed in. Such validation would be reported with reference to the TRIPOD+AI statement \cite{Collins_2024}.
\item A clinical model that includes the PR interval and the variables of a full clinical score would sharpen the comparison with the clinical model of this study.
\item A paired interval for the difference between the fused and the clinical model would show whether the one-year gain exceeds sampling variation.
\item An occlusion readout on held-out ECGs, with replacements other than zero, would show how far the PR-window profile depends on the choices of the present readout.
\end{itemize}

ops.rationale: Names the model the fused model, and replaces 'agreed closely in most risk deciles' with the decile values the Results report; no number added.
ops.new_text: On ICD-coded hospital diagnoses linked to MIMIC-IV-ECG, the fused model, a block-term tensor network with a separate clinical term, had the highest one-year discrimination of the methods compared. Its AUROC was 0.7776, against 0.7597 for the clinical model and 0.7350 for a CNN. Without refitting for each horizon, it kept its point estimates above those of the clinical model at horizons from 120 days to five years after the index ECG. After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, its mean predicted one-year risk was 0.61\% in the lowest risk decile and 12.3\% in the highest, against observed proportions of 0.55\% and 11.4\%. The largest gap, in the sixth decile, was 4.95\% observed against 3.56\% predicted. The fused model also flagged more future cases than the clinical model at each flagged fraction. Its gain over the clinical model is small, and the one-year intervals overlap. The gain is consistent in direction within one health system, and no interval for the difference yet establishes it.

ops.rationale: Writes 'The ECG term alone' as ECG-only BTTN, the name the Method gives it.
ops.new_text: ECG-only BTTN reached the discrimination of a compact CNN under the same protocol, while its evidence passes through frequency and lead factors that lie on the predictive path and can be read. The clinical term adds the risk factors without passing through those factors. Per unit of signal energy, the ECG term responded most to the PR window of the beat. This is the part of the cardiac cycle that cohort studies of the PR interval tie to later AF \cite{Cheng_2009,Magnani_2013}. The readout describes the fitted model, and its atrial reading remains a hypothesis.

ops.rationale: Writes 'the ECG term alone' as ECG-only BTTN and 'clinical comparator' as clinical model.
ops.new_text: For the design of ECG risk models, the results suggest that a clinical term kept outside the block-term factors adds to the discrimination of the ECG term. At one year, the fused model reached 0.7776 [0.7664, 0.7888] and ECG-only BTTN 0.7397 [0.7275, 0.7517]. These two intervals do not overlap, although the study reports no paired interval for this difference. The clinical model used here is narrower than a full clinical score, and the readout is descriptive. Validation outside one health system, a test of the factors on ICD-coded labels and a clinical model that includes the PR interval are the next requirements before any clinical use.

ops.rationale: Opens the paragraph on its point, the energy-normalised profile highest in the PR window, and follows it with the raw QRS dominance and its cause; every value, claim and reference kept.
ops.new_text: Per unit of energy removed, the occlusion profile of the ECG term was highest in the PR window, at 0.00216 (Table~\ref{tab:occlusion}). The ST window (0.00157), the P window (0.00152) and the T window (0.00127) followed, and the QRS window was lowest (0.00086). The P and ST windows were close to each other. Raw occlusion was instead dominated by the QRS window, where the mean drop in log-risk was 0.0232 against 0.0037 in the PR window. The QRS complex has the highest amplitude of the beat, so zeroing it removes the most energy and changes the spectrogram most. Figure~\ref{fig:beat-saliency} shows the energy-normalised response on the mean median beat of each lead. The profile describes what the fitted ECG term responds to on 120 high-risk training ECGs.
